claim: Seminal plasma is the only human biological fluid known to contain endogenous amyloid fibrils in a non-disease state.
source: Thus far, SP is also the only human biological fluid known to contain endogenous amyloid fibrils in a non-disease state (Usmani et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Usmani et al., 2014

claim: Two classes of semen amyloids have been identified: those derived from proteolytic fragments of prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) which polymerize to form amyloids named SEVI, and those derived from PSA-generated fragments of semenogelins which polymerize to form amyloids named SEM fibrils.
source: Two classes of semen amyloids have been identified: those derived from proteolytic fragments of prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) which polymerize to form amyloids named semen-derived enhancer of viral infection (SEVI), and those derived from PSA-generated fragments of semenogelins which polymerize to form amyloids named SEM fibrils.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about semen amyloid classification

claim: Both SEVI and SEM amyloids markedly enhance HIV infection by electrostatically binding HIV virions and increasing their propensity to bind to and infect cellular targets.
source: Both sets of amyloids markedly enhance HIV infection by electrostatically binding HIV virions and increasing their propensity to bind to and infect cellular targets (Münch et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010; Roan et al., 2011; Arnold et al., 2012; Roan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The ability of semen and seminal plasma to enhance HIV infection directly correlates with endogenous levels of semen amyloid fibrils.
source: Because the ability of semen and SP to enhance HIV infection directly correlates with endogenous levels of these fibrils (Kim et al., 2010; Roan et al., 2014), inhibiting the activity of semen amyloids may decrease HIV transmission rates.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2010 and Roan et al., 2014

claim: Semen fibrils are currently being pursued as targets for HIV microbicide development.
source: Indeed, semen fibrils are currently being pursued as targets for HIV microbicide development (Olsen et al., 2010; Roan et al., 2010; Hartjen et al., 2012; Lump et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on microbicide development

claim: SEM proteins have undergone extensive positive selection over evolutionary time.
source: SEM proteins have undergone extensive positive selection over evolutionary time (Hurle et al., 2007; Ferreira et al., 2013), suggesting an important role for these proteins in evolutionary fitness.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hurle et al., 2007 and Ferreira et al., 2013

claim: The amyloidogenic potential of SEM peptides and their virus-enhancing properties are conserved amongst great apes.
source: Studies analyzing orthologs of the human amyloidogenic SEM peptide from 12 non-human primate species revealed that the amyloidogenic potential of these orthologous peptides and their virus-enhancing properties are conserved amongst great apes (Roan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roan et al., 2014

claim: Seminal plasma amyloids promote infection by multiple sexually transmitted viruses.
source: Furthermore, the observation that SP amyloids promote infection by multiple sexually transmitted viruses (Tang et al., 2013; Torres et al., 2015) suggests that they should be selected against during primate evolution unless they serve a significant physiological purpose.
evidence: Supported by citations to Tang et al., 2013 and Torres et al., 2015

claim: SEVI and SEM fibrils decreased in vitro fertilization rates in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, both SEVI and SEM fibrils decreased IVF rates in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: Significant inhibition of IVF was observed at fibril concentrations of 50 µg/ml, and near complete inhibition was achieved with 250 µg/ml.
source: Significant inhibition of IVF was observed at fibril concentrations of 50 µg/ml, and near complete inhibition was achieved with 250 µg/ml.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from IVF assays

claim: Concentrations of amyloidogenic peptides in semen range from 28 to 267 µg/ml.
source: Because concentrations of amyloidogenic peptides in semen range from 28 to 267 µg/ml (Münch et al., 2007; Roan et al., 2011, 2014), these results suggest that physiologically relevant concentrations of semen fibrils suppress IVF.
evidence: Supported by citations to Münch et al., 2007; Roan et al., 2011, 2014

claim: Physiologically relevant concentrations of semen fibrils suppress IVF.
source: Because concentrations of amyloidogenic peptides in semen range from 28 to 267 µg/ml (Münch et al., 2007; Roan et al., 2011, 2014), these results suggest that physiologically relevant concentrations of semen fibrils suppress IVF.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental concentrations with physiological concentrations

claim: The inhibition of IVF by semen fibrils was not due to fibril-induced cytotoxicity to the spermatozoa, oocytes, or embryos.
source: This inhibition was not due to fibril-induced cytotoxicity to the spermatozoa, oocytes, or embryos, as evidenced by propidium iodide (PI) staining experiments (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by propidium iodide staining experiments

claim: Semen fibrils inhibit fusion of sperm to oocyte by entrapping mouse sperm cells.
source: To clarify the mechanism underlying reduced IVF rates in the presence of the fibrils, we performed live cell imaging. We found that the fibrils seem to inhibit fusion of sperm to oocyte by entrapping mouse sperm cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Video 1

claim: Fibrils entrapped human spermatozoa in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Fibrils similarly entrapped human spermatozoa in a dose-dependent manner, as assessed by both manual quantitation as well as computer-assisted sperm analysis (CASA) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Semen fibrils directly interact with the plasma membranes of both sperm heads and tails.
source: Close examination of fibril-exposed human spermatozoa by cryosection electron microscopy revealed that the fibrils directly interacted with the plasma membranes of both sperm heads and tails, and that points of contact tended to extend the membrane away from the base of the sperm head and tail (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Purified endogenous amyloids from human seminal plasma associate with spermatozoa.
source: Microscopic analysis showed that these purified endogenous amyloids associated with spermatozoa, as did endogenous amyloids present in fresh liquefied ejaculates (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Purified endogenous amyloids efficiently entrapped spermatozoa.
source: Furthermore, purified endogenous amyloids, like synthetic fibrils, efficiently entrapped spermatozoa (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Within 10 minutes after perfusion of SEM fibrils, some spermatozoa became completely immotile, while others exhibited twitching movements.
source: Remarkably, within 10 min after perfusion of the SEM fibrils, some spermatozoa became completely immotile, while others exhibited twitching movements (Video 2B, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by video microscopy data shown in Video 2B and Figure 2D

claim: In the presence of semen fibrils, 89.8 ± 9.3% of spermatozoa were fully or partly immobilized.
source: In the presence of the fibrils, 89.8 ± 9.3% of spermatozoa (average data from three donors) were fully or partly immobilized as defined by at least 50% of the tail being surface-immobilized.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of video microscopy data from three donors

claim: SEM fibril-induced immobilization did not cause changes in propidium iodide uptake, mitochondrial activity, or ability to capacitate relative to control peptide.
source: SEM fibril-induced immobilization did not cause changes in PI uptake, mitochondrial activity, or ability to capacitate relative to control peptide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), showing that immobilized spermatozoa were not compromised in viability due to exposure to amyloid structures.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Perfusion of seminal proteases onto fibril-immobilized spermatozoa partially restored sperm motility.
source: In addition, perfusion of seminal proteases onto fibril-immobilized spermatozoa partially restored sperm motility (Video 3) further confirming lack of cytotoxicity.
evidence: Supported by video microscopy data shown in Video 3

claim: SEM1(68–85), a naturally-occurring SEM-derived peptide in semen that does not form fibrils, did not inhibit sperm motility.
source: We further demonstrated that the ability of SEM fibrils to immobilize spermatozoa was linked to its fibrillar structure by showing that SEM1(68–85), a naturally-occurring SEM-derived peptide in semen that does not form fibrils (Roan et al., 2011), did not inhibit motility (Video 4A, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Video 4A and Figure 2D, with citation to Roan et al., 2011

claim: SEM1(108–159), a SEM-derived peptide that is non-fibrillar but highly cationic, did not inhibit sperm motility.
source: Motility was also not inhibited by SEM1(108–159), a SEM-derived peptide that is non-fibrillar but highly cationic (pI = 10.12) (Roan et al., 2011) (Video 4B, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Video 4B and Figure 2D, with citation to Roan et al., 2011

claim: Human SEVI and the SEM-derived fibril from Otolemur garnettii (Galago) both immobilized spermatozoa.
source: In contrast, human SEVI (Münch et al., 2007) and the previously described SEM-derived fibril from the non-human primate Otolemur garnettii (referred to as Galago) (Roan et al., 2014) both immobilized spermatozoa (Video 5A,B, Figure 2D), while Aβ(1–42) fibrils, not naturally present in semen, did not cause immobilization (Video 5C, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Video 5A,B and Figure 2D, with citations to Münch et al., 2007 and Roan et al., 2014

claim: Aβ(1–42) fibrils, not naturally present in semen, did not cause immobilization of spermatozoa.
source: In contrast, human SEVI (Münch et al., 2007) and the previously described SEM-derived fibril from the non-human primate Otolemur garnettii (referred to as Galago) (Roan et al., 2014) both immobilized spermatozoa (Video 5A,B, Figure 2D), while Aβ(1–42) fibrils, not naturally present in semen, did not cause immobilization (Video 5C, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Video 5C and Figure 2D

claim: Semen amyloid fibrils, and not native semen peptides or pathological amyloids, are distinct in their ability to immobilize sperm cells.
source: All together, these data suggest that semen amyloid fibrils, and not native semen peptides or pathological amyloids, are distinct in their ability to immobilize sperm cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of effects of different peptides and fibrils on sperm motility

claim: Sexual intercourse elicits a massive infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages into the female reproductive tract.
source: Sexual intercourse elicits a massive infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages into the female reproductive tract (FRT) (Pandya and Cohen, 1985; Sharkey et al., 2012), presumably to mediate clearance of microorganisms and remnant sperm cells, and perhaps to filter out morphologically abnormal and/or non-functional sperm cells (Tomlinson et al., 1992; Oren-Benaroya et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pandya and Cohen, 1985 and Sharkey et al., 2012

claim: Addition of semen fibrils markedly increased phagocytosis of spermatozoa by macrophages.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, phagocytosis of spermatozoa was apparent by 3 hr, and markedly increased by semen fibrils.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Addition of semen fibrils increased phagocytosis of spermatozoa from 4.61% to 22.6%.
source: Consistent with the Western blot data, addition of fibrils increased phagocytosis of spermatozoa, from 4.61% to 22.6% (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Sperm cells damaged by multiple freeze/thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen or electromagnetic radiation were taken up at higher rates than healthy sperm cells.
source: Sperm cells damaged by multiple freeze/thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen or electromagnetic radiation were taken up at higher rates than healthy sperm cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A

claim: In the absence of fibrils, the rate of phagocytosis of liquid nitrogen-damaged spermatozoa was higher than that of fresh spermatozoa (31.3% versus 4.61%).
source: In the absence of the fibrils, the rate of phagocytosis of liquid nitrogen-damaged spermatozoa was higher than that of fresh spermatozoa (31.3% versus 4.61%, respectively); this was also observed in the presence of the fibrils but at higher percentages (49.9% versus 22.6%, respectively) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: In the presence of fibrils, the rate of phagocytosis of liquid nitrogen-damaged spermatozoa was higher than that of fresh spermatozoa (49.9% versus 22.6%).
source: In the absence of the fibrils, the rate of phagocytosis of liquid nitrogen-damaged spermatozoa was higher than that of fresh spermatozoa (31.3% versus 4.61%, respectively); this was also observed in the presence of the fibrils but at higher percentages (49.9% versus 22.6%, respectively) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Semen fibrils promote the kinetics of sperm phagocytosis.
source: Interestingly, with longer incubation times high levels of phagocytosis of both healthy and damaged sperm cells were achieved in the presence of fibrils, suggesting that the fibrils promote the kinetics of sperm phagocytosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Inferred from time-course data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: Semen fibrils increased the number of spermatozoa engulfed by individual macrophages, frequently resulting in a single macrophage endocytosing more than a dozen sperm heads.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed that fibrils also increased the number of spermatozoa engulfed by individual macrophages, frequently resulting in a single macrophage endocytosing more than a dozen sperm heads (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Videos 8 and 9).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Videos 8 and 9

claim: In the presence of semen fibrils, damaged spermatozoa are preferentially phagocytosed over healthy ones.
source: We consistently observed in multiple donors that in the presence of the fibrils damaged spermatozoa are preferentially phagocytosed over healthy ones (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from multiple donors shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A

claim: Macrophages preferentially phagocytose damaged spermatozoa both in the absence and presence of semen fibrils.
source: We found that although damaged spermatozoa were preferentially phagocytosed both in the absence and presence of the fibrils, the highest rate of damaged sperm phagocytosis occurred in the presence of fibrils, when 36.8% of macrophages contained damaged spermatozoa (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5

claim: The highest rate of damaged sperm phagocytosis occurred in the presence of fibrils, when 36.8% of macrophages contained damaged spermatozoa.
source: We found that although damaged spermatozoa were preferentially phagocytosed both in the absence and presence of the fibrils, the highest rate of damaged sperm phagocytosis occurred in the presence of fibrils, when 36.8% of macrophages contained damaged spermatozoa (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5

claim: Spermatozoa are highly prone to undergo apoptosis, and this process is accelerated by reactive oxygen species produced by surrounding leukocytes as well as the sperm cells themselves.
source: Spermatozoa are highly prone to undergo apoptosis, and this process is accelerated by reactive oxygen species produced by surrounding leukocytes as well as the sperm cells themselves (Aitken et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aitken et al., 2012

claim: Incubation of swim-up sperm cells for 24 hr at 25°C increases the proportion of apoptotic sperm cells.
source: Annexin V staining confirmed that compared to fresh sperm cells, a higher proportion of the 24 hour-treated sperm cells were apoptotic (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: The highest levels of phagocytosis of apoptotic sperm cells was observed under conditions where semen fibrils were present.
source: Like damaged spermatozoa, the highest levels of phagocytosis of apoptotic sperm cells was observed under conditions where semen fibrils were present (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Semen fibrils promote phagocytosis of sperm cells by macrophages.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate that semen fibrils promote phagocytosis of sperm cells by macrophages.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results

claim: The semen fibrils may participate in quality control by promoting the efficiency of sperm selection by macrophages.
source: Because the highest rates of damaged sperm phagocytosis occurred in the presence of semen fibrils, the fibrils may participate in quality control by promoting the efficiency of sperm selection by macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of preferential phagocytosis of damaged sperm in presence of fibrils

claim: By promoting phagocytosis of non-damaged sperm, the fibrils appear to additionally participate in rapidly clearing the lower reproductive tract of remaining sperm cells.
source: Moreover, by also promoting phagocytosis of non-damaged sperm, the fibrils appear to additionally participate in rapidly clearing the lower reproductive tract of remaining sperm cells (whether damaged or not), which may help avoid the development of an inappropriate cell-mediated immune response against sperm antigens.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and reasoning about immune response

claim: The rapid removal of sperm cells is consistent with the observation that the lower reproductive tract largely returns to its pre-mating state by 24 hr post-coitus.
source: The rapid removal of sperm cells is consistent with the observation that the lower reproductive tract largely returns to its pre-mating state by 24 hr post-coitus (Pandya and Cohen, 1985), and may help explain why only a minute fraction of deposited spermatozoa actually reach the oviduct isthmus (Hunter, 1993; Eisenbach and Giojalas, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pandya and Cohen, 1985; Hunter, 1993; Eisenbach and Giojalas, 2006

claim: Only a minute fraction of deposited spermatozoa actually reach the oviduct isthmus.
source: The rapid removal of sperm cells is consistent with the observation that the lower reproductive tract largely returns to its pre-mating state by 24 hr post-coitus (Pandya and Cohen, 1985), and may help explain why only a minute fraction of deposited spermatozoa actually reach the oviduct isthmus (Hunter, 1993; Eisenbach and Giojalas, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunter, 1993 and Eisenbach and Giojalas, 2006

claim: High concentrations of spermatozoa can result in increased polyploidy rates and be detrimental for human embryonic development.
source: This in turn may be important for fertilization and blastocyst development since high concentrations of spermatozoa can result in increased polyploidy rates and be detrimental for human embryonic development (Mahadevan and Trounson, 1984; Diamond et al., 1985; Englert et al., 1986; Dumoulin et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mahadevan and Trounson, 1984; Diamond et al., 1985; Englert et al., 1986; Dumoulin et al., 1992

claim: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) have been shown to entrap spermatozoa.
source: Of note, semen fibrils may not be the only structures in semen that can participate in sperm disposal; neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) – chromatin- and protein-containing extracellular fibers extruded by neutrophils to trap and kill bacteria (Brinkmann et al., 2004) – have been shown to entrap spermatozoa (Alghamdi and Foster, 2005), which could conceivably promote their subsequent phagocytic uptake.
evidence: Supported by citations to Brinkmann et al., 2004 and Alghamdi and Foster, 2005

claim: NETs inhibit rather than enhance HIV infection.
source: Importantly, however, NETs are different from the semen fibrils because they inhibit rather than enhance HIV infection (Saitoh et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saitoh et al., 2012

claim: Amyloid fibrils have long been considered a result of aberrant protein folding that is almost exclusively associated with systemic or localized amyloidosis, or various chronic degenerative diseases.
source: Amyloid fibrils have long been considered a result of aberrant protein folding that is almost exclusively associated with systemic or localized amyloidosis, or various chronic degenerative diseases (Chiti and Dobson, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chiti and Dobson, 2006

claim: It is becoming increasingly clear that fibrils may also form for beneficial reasons.
source: However, it is becoming increasingly clear that fibrils may also form for beneficial reasons (Kelly and Balch, 2003; Hou et al., 2011; Bergman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kelly and Balch, 2003; Hou et al., 2011; Bergman et al., 2016

claim: HD6 (human α-defensin 6) forms amyloid nets to protect host cells from invasion by enteric bacterial pathogens.
source: Two prominent examples of functional amyloid in humans are HD6 (human α-defensin 6) forming amyloid nets to protect host cells from invasion by enteric bacterial pathogens (Chu et al., 2012), and Pmel17 fibrils facilitating the formation of melanosomes with covalently linked melanin (Fowler et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chu et al., 2012

claim: Pmel17 fibrils facilitate the formation of melanosomes with covalently linked melanin.
source: Two prominent examples of functional amyloid in humans are HD6 (human α-defensin 6) forming amyloid nets to protect host cells from invasion by enteric bacterial pathogens (Chu et al., 2012), and Pmel17 fibrils facilitating the formation of melanosomes with covalently linked melanin (Fowler et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fowler et al., 2006

claim: Prior studies have suggested that amyloids generated by the male reproductive tract may play beneficial roles in bacterial clearance and sperm maturation.
source: Prior studies have also suggested that amyloids generated by the male reproductive tract may play beneficial roles in bacterial clearance and sperm maturation (Whelly et al., 2012; Easterhoff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Whelly et al., 2012 and Easterhoff et al., 2013

claim: The present findings add SEVI and SEM fibrils to the growing list of functional amyloids in humans by demonstrating that these fibrils can play an active role in defective sperm disposal.
source: The present findings add SEVI and SEM fibrils to the growing list of functional amyloids in humans by demonstrating that these fibrils can play an active role in defective sperm disposal.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript

claim: Synthetic SEVI and SEM peptides form fibrils as confirmed by thioflavin T staining and electron microscopy.
source: Synthetic SEVI and SEM peptides were confirmed to form fibrils by thioflavin T (ThT) staining and electron microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ThT staining and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Synthetic semen fibrils include both fibrils and fibrillar oligomers as well as prefibrillar oligomers.
source: These synthetic fibrils, like their endogenous counterparts, include both fibrils and fibrillar oligomers as well as prefibrillar oligomers, as determined by their reactivity with amyloid conformer-specific antibodies OC and A11 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by antibody reactivity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Endogenous semen fibrils behave similarly to synthetic versions of the fibrils.
source: Because endogenous semen fibrils behave similarly to synthetic versions of the fibrils and are difficult to isolate as purified materials (Roan et al., 2014; Usmani et al., 2014), we used fibrils derived from synthetic peptides for the majority of our studies.
evidence: Supported by citations to Roan et al., 2014 and Usmani et al., 2014

claim: The infection-promoting effects of semen fibrils are driven by electrostatic forces and are not receptor-specific.
source: Given that the infection-promoting effects of the fibrils are driven by electrostatic forces and is not receptor-specific (Roan et al., 2009, 2011), if fertilization is enhanced by the fibrils, then the effect should be species-independent.
evidence: Supported by citations to Roan et al., 2009, 2011

claim: The immobilization of sperm by SEM fibrils is distinct from the previously described ability of the SEM1 holoprotein to limit sperm motility by binding to the sperm-associated EPPIN complex.
source: Of note, this immobilization is distinct from the previously described ability of the SEM1 holoprotein to limit sperm motility by binding to the sperm-associated EPPIN complex (Mitra et al., 2010), since that activity, mapped to cysteine 239 of SEM1, is not part of the amyloidogenic SEM1 fragment (Roan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitra et al., 2010 and Roan et al., 2014

claim: Proteolytic degradation of amyloidogenic peptides in semen occurs gradually over the course of liquefaction.
source: Because proteolytic degradation of amyloidogenic peptides in semen occurs gradually over the course of liquefaction (Roan et al., 2014), immobilization of sperm is likely most efficient during the earliest stages post-ejaculation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Roan et al., 2014

claim: Immobilization of sperm by semen fibrils is likely most efficient during the earliest stages post-ejaculation.
source: Because proteolytic degradation of amyloidogenic peptides in semen occurs gradually over the course of liquefaction (Roan et al., 2014), immobilization of sperm is likely most efficient during the earliest stages post-ejaculation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that proteolytic degradation occurs gradually

claim: The differential effects of semen fibrils vs. Aβ(1–42) fibrils on sperm motility could be due to differences in fibril charge and/or distribution of amyloid conformers.
source: The differential effects of semen fibrils vs. Aβ(1–42) fibrils on sperm motility could be due to differences in fibril charge and/or distribution of amyloid conformers.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms underlying observed differences

claim: Increased levels of macrophages are associated with decreased levels of abnormal spermatozoa in semen.
source: All together, these results suggest that: (1) macrophages preferentially phagocytose damaged spermatozoa both in the absence and presence of semen fibrils, consistent with prior reports that increased levels of macrophages are associated with decreased levels of abnormal spermatozoa in semen (Tomlinson et al., 1992), and (2) within the first hour, the highest levels of damaged sperm phagocytosis are observed in the presence of semen fibrils.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tomlinson et al., 1992

claim: Within the first hour, the highest levels of damaged sperm phagocytosis are observed in the presence of semen fibrils.
source: All together, these results suggest that: (1) macrophages preferentially phagocytose damaged spermatozoa both in the absence and presence of semen fibrils, consistent with prior reports that increased levels of macrophages are associated with decreased levels of abnormal spermatozoa in semen (Tomlinson et al., 1992), and (2) within the first hour, the highest levels of damaged sperm phagocytosis are observed in the presence of semen fibrils.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing time-dependent phagocytosis

claim: All known semen fibrils are highly cationic and bind to anionic membrane components.
source: Because all known semen fibrils are highly cationic and bind to anionic membrane components (Roan et al., 2009, 2011), we reasoned they may also entrap and promote phagocytosis of apoptotic sperm cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to Roan et al., 2009, 2011

claim: Swim-up sperm cells are prone to undergo their default cascade of apoptotic cell death when no longer in the antioxidant environment of seminal plasma.
source: Because swim-up sperm cells are no longer in the antioxidant environment of seminal plasma, they are prone to undergo their default cascade of apoptotic cell death (Aitken et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aitken et al., 2012

claim: One of the hallmarks of apoptotic sperm cells is externalization of phosphatidylserine, a negatively charged phospholipid membrane component.
source: One of the hallmarks of apoptotic sperm cells is externalization of phosphatidylserine, a negatively charged phospholipid membrane component.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about apoptotic cells
